title: Genus of a hyperelliptic curve
notes: The motivating example is \(y^2=P_n(x)\), with \(P_n\) squarefree, and genus \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\); degrees three and four give one handle and degrees five and six give two.
statement: Over \(\mathbb C\), let \(P\) be a squarefree polynomial of degree \(n\geq1\). The smooth projective model of \(y^2=P(x)\) has genus \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\). Indeed, its degree-two map to \(\mathbb P^1\) has \(n\) finite simple branch points and one further branch point at infinity exactly when \(n\) is odd; Riemann--Hurwitz gives the formula.
reconstruction: The genus belongs to the smooth compact model. The branch count supplies an elementary proof and includes the point at infinity.
fate: This is a classical hyperelliptic genus calculation. It also follows from the Newton-polygon genus theorem read in \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1978genus}; that publication predates this explanatory talk.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Degree genus formula and why the hyperelliptic plane model is special
notes: The notes give \((n-1)(n-2)/2\) for a general degree-\(n\) equation, then say that the hyperelliptic equation is “not an equation of degree \(n\)”.
statement: A nonsingular plane projective curve of degree \(d\) has genus \((d-1)(d-2)/2\). For \(n\geq2\), \(y^2-P_n(x)\) does have total degree \(n\); its projective closure is a special degree-\(n\) model, generally singular at infinity, so the nonsingular plane-curve formula cannot simply be applied to that model.
reconstruction: The intended distinction is generic versus special support, not total degree. Passing to normalization explains the discrepancy in genera.
fate: This is the classical plane genus formula. Its realization as the count of interior lattice points of the degree-\(d\) triangle is covered by \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1978genus} and the speaker's later explicit comparison in \citet[slides 6--8]{khovanskii2025chern}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Newton polygons and Laurent-monomial translation
notes: The Newton polygon is the convex hull of exponent pairs with nonzero coefficients. Multiplication by \(x^ay^b\) translates it; the curve is considered away from the coordinate cross.
statement: For a nonzero Laurent polynomial \(P=\sum_{m\in A}c_mx^m\) on \(T=(\mathbb C^*)^n\), define \(\Delta(P)=\operatorname{conv}\{m:c_m\ne0\}\subset\mathbb R^n\). Since a Laurent monomial is a unit on \(T\), multiplying by it leaves the torus zero scheme unchanged and translates \(\Delta(P)\) by the exponent vector.
reconstruction: The torus restriction is essential: multiplication by a polynomial monomial can add coordinate-axis components in affine space.
fate: The definition and its character-lattice interpretation are read in \citet[\S\S1--2]{khovanskii1977toroidal}, published in 1977. These are already established tools in the 1981 lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The Newton-polygon genus theorem
notes: The answer to the first motivating question is the number of interior lattice points of the Newton polygon, for coefficients in general position; the notebook attributes the earlier result to Baker and its rediscovery to Khovanskii.
statement: Let \(P\in\mathbb C[x^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]\) have a two-dimensional Newton polygon \(\Delta\), and assume its torus curve is irreducible and Newton nondegenerate: for every face \(F\), including \(\Delta\), the equations \(P_F=x\partial_xP_F=y\partial_yP_F=0\) have no common solution in \((\mathbb C^*)^2\). The genus of its smooth projective model is \(\#(\operatorname{int}\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\). Generic coefficients with prescribed full Newton polygon satisfy these hypotheses.
reconstruction: Face nondegeneracy and the smooth projective model make “general position” precise. The historical teacher--student anecdote is not needed for the theorem and was not independently verified.
fate: The exact hypersurface genus result is read in \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1978genus}; its companion paper \citet[\S2]{khovanskii1977toroidal} defines nondegeneracy and the good toric compactification. Thus the talk is exposition of published 1977--1978 work, not a new unresolved genus question.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Boundary valuations and unimodular monomial changes
notes: At an omitted point, the orders of \(x,y\) give an integral vector. A monomial substitution with determinant one changes this vector by the corresponding integral matrix; primitive vectors can be made coordinate vectors.
statement: On the smooth compactification of an irreducible torus curve, each boundary point \(p\) has \(v_p=(\operatorname{ord}_p x,\operatorname{ord}_p y)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}\). Under \(x=u^{a_{11}}v^{a_{12}},\ y=u^{a_{21}}v^{a_{22}}\), the order column is multiplied by \(A\). For \(A\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)\), the map is an isomorphism of tori. Any primitive lattice vector is carried to a coordinate vector by such a matrix. In the nondegenerate compactification the boundary order vectors are primitive inward edge normals.
reconstruction: The determinant may be either \(1\) or \(-1\); the written determinant-one subcase is sufficient. Primitivity of boundary vectors uses transverse intersection with the toric boundary and cannot be assumed for arbitrary singular curves.
fate: The lattice duality and admissible smooth toric charts are read in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; its \S2 gives the transverse compactification for nondegenerate systems.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Edge lengths count punctures
notes: After translating an edge to a coordinate axis, its polynomial has as many nonzero roots as the length of the edge, with distinct roots in general position. A later sentence instead says “number of lattice points on the segment”; the total puncture count is the number of boundary lattice points.
statement: Under the nondegeneracy hypotheses of 1980-509.4, the compactified curve meets the toric divisor associated to an edge \(E\) in exactly its lattice length \(\ell(E)=\#(E\cap\mathbb Z^2)-1\) distinct transverse points. Consequently the number of punctures of the curve in \((\mathbb C^*)^2\) is \(\sum_E\ell(E)=\#(\partial\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\). Vertex initial polynomials are monomials and contribute no roots.
reconstruction: The local edge count and the global boundary-point count differ by one per closed edge because vertices are counted twice in the latter edgewise listing. Simple roots supply the transverse local parameter.
fate: This is the elementary boundary calculation in the nondegenerate toric compactification of \citet[\S\S1--2]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; the speaker states the exact curve count again in \citet[slide 6]{khovanskii2025chern}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Divisor degree and the signed boundary root count
notes: The notes restrict \(Q\) to \(P=0\), say its divisor is zero, substitute \(x\sim t^n,y\sim t^m\), and sum minimum scalar products over punctures to count the torus roots.
statement: Let \(C\) be the smooth projective model of \(P=0\) and let \(Q|_C\) be a nonzero meromorphic function. Then \(\deg\operatorname{div}(Q|_C)=0\), not generally \(\operatorname{div}(Q|_C)=0\). If the initial terms of \(Q\) do not cancel at a boundary point \(p\), its order is \(\min_{a\in\Delta(Q)}\langle a,v_p\rangle\). As \(Q\) has no poles in the torus, the number of its torus zeros, with multiplicity, is \[-\sum_{p\in C\setminus T}\operatorname{ord}_p(Q)=-\sum_{p\in C\setminus T}\min_{a\in\Delta(Q)}\langle a,v_p\rangle.\]
reconstruction: The missing minus sign and the difference between a divisor and its degree are explicit corrections. Local expansions have nonvanishing unit factors and the right-hand side of equation (11) requires the full sum; the minimum formula needs noncancellation of its leading coefficient.
fate: The valuation and intersection mechanism is already present in \citet[\S\S1--2]{khovanskii1977toroidal} and the root-count application in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1978genus}. The sign is checked directly from the degree-zero identity.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Mixed area and the two incompatible normalizations
notes: The planar coefficient \(S(K,L)\) is defined by \(\operatorname{Area}(aK+bL)=a^2\operatorname{Area}(K)+b^2\operatorname{Area}(L)+abS(K,L)\). The following general definition instead sets \(V(K,\ldots,K)=\operatorname{Vol}(K)\).
statement: The standard mixed volume is the symmetric Minkowski-multilinear functional with \(V(K,\ldots,K)=\operatorname{Vol}_n(K)\); equivalently, the coefficient of \(t_1\cdots t_n\) in \(\operatorname{Vol}(\sum t_iK_i)\) is \(n!V(K_1,\ldots,K_n)\). Thus \(S(K,L)=2V(K,L)=\operatorname{Area}(K+L)-\operatorname{Area}(K)-\operatorname{Area}(L)\), and \(S(K,K)=2\operatorname{Area}(K)\).
reconstruction: Symmetry and multilinearity in every slot are included in the characterization. The notebook shifts from the coefficient normalization \(S\) to the diagonal-volume normalization \(V\), so they cannot be substituted into root counts without the factorial.
fate: The exact polarization normalization is read in \citet[\S1, mixed-volume definition]{khovanskii1978genus} and \citet[slide 12]{khovanskii2025chern}. This is classical mixed-volume theory; the later lecture is an explicit normalization check.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Bernshtein’s torus root count, with multiplicities and nondegeneracy
notes: The second motivating question is answered by mixed area, and theorem (14), attributed to D. Bernshtein, states the generic system root count as the mixed volume of its Newton polytopes.
statement: For finite supports \(A_i\subset\mathbb Z^n\), put \(\Delta_i=\operatorname{conv}(A_i)\). A generic system of Laurent polynomials \(f_i\) with these Newton polytopes has \(n!V(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_n)\) isolated roots in \((\mathbb C^*)^n\), counted with multiplicity. A sufficient precise hypothesis for equality is that for every nonzero weight \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), the simultaneous initial system \(f_{1,w}=\cdots=f_{n,w}=0\) has no torus root and that the original system is zero-dimensional. In two variables the count is \(S(\Delta(P),\Delta(Q))\).
reconstruction: The torus, multiplicities, finite intersection, and nonzero-weight conditions are explicit. With the normalization immediately preceding theorem (14), its right-hand side lacks \(n!\), or lacks \(2\) in the stated planar case.
fate: \citet{bernshtein1975roots} was published in 1975 (received 7 April 1975; receipt is not a public-circulation date). The exact normalized theorem is read in \citet[\S1, number-of-solutions consequence]{khovanskii1978genus}. It is therefore known before this talk. Earlier 1974 Newton-polyhedron occurrences concern local singularity invariants and are not automatically the same problem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Equal polygons and the Bézout specialization
notes: When both polygons coincide, a support-distance sum equals twice their area; for the degree triangle this gives \(n^2\), identified with Bézout.
statement: Two generic torus polynomials with the same Newton polygon \(\Delta\) have \(2\operatorname{Area}(\Delta)\) common roots. For generic polynomials of total degrees \(d,e\), the polygons are \(d\Sigma,e\Sigma\), where \(\Sigma=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2)\); hence the mixed-area root count is \(de\). Genericity ensures that the projective Bézout intersections do not escape to coordinate divisors.
reconstruction: The displayed \(n^2\) is the equal-degree subcase. The support-distance formula is invariant under translation because the length-weighted outward normals sum to zero.
fate: This is the classical Bézout count recovered from the already published Bernshtein theorem; see \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1978genus}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Euler characteristic of a nondegenerate torus hypersurface
notes: The word “curve” is crossed out in favor of “hypersurface”, while equation (15) retains the constant negative sign \(-n!\operatorname{Vol}(\Delta)\).
statement: Let \(f\) have full-dimensional Newton polytope \(\Delta\subset\mathbb R^n\), and assume every face truncation, including the full polynomial, defines a smooth hypersurface in \((\mathbb C^*)^n\) when nonempty. Then \[\chi\{f=0\text{ in }(\mathbb C^*)^n\}=(-1)^{n-1}n!\operatorname{Vol}_n(\Delta).\] For complex algebraic varieties the ordinary and compactly supported Euler characteristics agree, although their cohomology groups do not generally agree.
reconstruction: The parity-dependent sign and the nondegeneracy assumption are supplied. The negative sign is correct for plane torus curves, but already fails for one-variable polynomials, whose zero set has positive cardinality.
fate: The exact result is read in \citet[\S3, Theorem 2 and hypersurface example]{khovanskii1978genus}. It was published three years before the seminar occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Pick’s formula from genus, punctures, and Euler characteristic
notes: Combining \(\chi=2-2B-\Gamma=-2S\), with \(B\) interior and \(\Gamma\) boundary lattice points, gives \(B+\Gamma/2=S+1\).
statement: For a two-dimensional convex lattice polygon \(\Delta\), write \(I=\#(\operatorname{int}\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\) and \(B=\#(\partial\Delta\cap\mathbb Z^2)\). Then \(\operatorname{Area}(\Delta)=I+B/2-1\). Choosing a generic nondegenerate torus curve gives genus \(I\), exactly \(B\) punctures, and Euler characteristic \(-2\operatorname{Area}(\Delta)\), which proves the identity.
reconstruction: Notation distinguishes the notebook's area \(S\) from its mixed-area coefficient. A generic curve exists for any such polygon; the formula is for the polygon itself.
fate: Pick's identity is classical. The same algebraic derivation is explicitly presented by the speaker in \citet[slides 6--7]{khovanskii2025chern}, and its ingredients were already published in \citet{khovanskii1978genus}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Mixed area with a disk and the isoperimetric inequality
notes: The mixed area of a polygon and the unit disk is its perimeter. The following inequality is written in the diagonal-volume normalization, \(V(K,L)^2\geq\operatorname{Area}(K)\operatorname{Area}(L)\), and equality for a disk is mentioned.
statement: For compact convex planar bodies \(K,L\) with nonempty interior, \(V(K,L)^2\geq\operatorname{Area}(K)\operatorname{Area}(L)\). If \(B\) is the unit disk, \(2V(K,B)=\operatorname{Perimeter}(K)\), because \(\operatorname{Area}(K+tB)=\operatorname{Area}(K)+t\operatorname{Perimeter}(K)+\pi t^2\). Hence \(\operatorname{Perimeter}(K)^2\geq4\pi\operatorname{Area}(K)\), with equality for disks.
reconstruction: The notebook's perimeter statement uses its coefficient normalization \(S=2V\). This accounts for the factor of four in the isoperimetric inequality; convexity and full planar dimension are explicit.
fate: These are established Minkowski and isoperimetric inequalities, not questions left open in 1981. The precise normalization and disk consequence are read in \citet[slide 12]{khovanskii2025chern}; the general Alexandrov--Fenchel statement is read in \citet[Theorem 2.1]{kavehkhovanskii2012equations}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The surface intersection inequality requires positivity
notes: For any two curves on any algebraic surface the notes claim \((\Gamma_1\cdot\Gamma_2)^2\geq\Gamma_1^2\Gamma_2^2\), citing the Hodge structure and relating it to mixed area.
statement: On a smooth projective complex surface, nef real divisor classes \(D,E\) satisfy \((D\cdot E)^2\geq D^2E^2\), by the Hodge index theorem and approximation by ample classes. The assertion for arbitrary curves is false: the two disjoint exceptional curves on the blow-up of \(\mathbb P^2\) at two distinct points have squares \(-1\) and mutual intersection zero. For globally generated toric divisors associated to polygons, \(D_K\cdot D_L=2V(K,L)\), which gives the mixed-area inequality.
reconstruction: Smoothness, projectivity, and positivity are substantive hypotheses. The exceptional-curve example is a direct diagnostic counterexample, not a historical attribution. The last toric identity requires a common smooth projective refinement of the polygons' normal fans.
fate: The surface Hodge inequality is classical. The exact positive-form version and its proof are read in \citet[Corollary 7.11]{kavehkhovanskii2010mixed}; the same paper explains the toric intersection/mixed-volume correspondence in \S2. The later work broadens the intersection theory but does not make the unrestricted notebook assertion true.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Toric compactification from compatible monomial charts
notes: The end of the talk begins a compactification by monomial changes of coordinates and cones, explaining how a curve or divisor becomes visible at the boundary.
statement: A finite fan \(\Sigma\) of strongly convex rational polyhedral cones in the cocharacter lattice defines a normal toric variety by gluing \(U_\sigma=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\sigma^\vee\cap M]\) along their face charts. When every cone is generated by part of a lattice basis, the variety is smooth. A complete fan gives a compact complex toric variety. Refining the normal fan of the Newton polytopes supplies a compactification in which nondegenerate complete intersections meet torus strata transversely.
reconstruction: Compatibility means that every cone intersection is a common face and all faces are included; mere disjointness of maximal-cone interiors does not suffice. The later 23 February occurrence supplies the fuller chart and completeness discussion.
fate: The exact construction and admissibility/completeness theorems are read in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}, and the systematic fan construction in \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric}. Both sources were explicitly available before this lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Dixmier’s commuting operators of orders four and six
notes: Two monic polynomial-coefficient operators of orders four and six commute but are not both functions of a single operator of order two; the note writes a square-root relation.
statement: In the first Weyl algebra over \(\mathbb C\), there exist commuting ordinary differential operators of orders \(4,6\), rank \(2\), whose joint spectral curve is an elliptic cubic. The rank-two qualification concerns the generic common eigenspace, not merely the greatest common divisor of the two displayed orders.
fate: This is the 1968 Dixmier example, revisited explicitly on P000970; see \citet{dixmier1968weyl}. The corrected operators and their algebraic identity are checked in the development section.

title: KdV inverse scattering and the recorded Lax pair
notes: Stage I displays \(u_t=6uu_x+u_{xxx}\), \(L=D^2-u\), \(A=D^3-uD-Du\), and \([L,A]=L_t\).
statement: For a smooth scalar function \(u\), a consistent normalization is \(L=D^2+u\), \(A=-4D^3-3(uD+Du)\), and \(L_t=[L,A]\), which yields \(u_t=6uu_x+u_{xxx}\). For sufficiently decaying real potentials the associated one-dimensional scattering data supply the inverse-scattering variables.
reconstruction: The signs and factors in \(L,A\) are an explicit emendation. The decay conditions belong to the scattering interpretation, not to the purely differential-operator identity.
fate: The isospectral method precedes the talk; see \citet[pp.~467--490]{lax1968integrals}. Direct use of \(Df=fD+f^{\prime}\) shows that the notebook’s three displayed formulas do not form this Lax pair.

title: Matrix zero-curvature equations
notes: Stage II uses \([D_x-U,D_t-V]=0\), with \(U,V\) rational in the spectral parameter; an example has degrees two and one.
statement: For matrix-valued \(U(x,t,\lambda),V(x,t,\lambda)\), compatibility of \(\psi_x=U\psi\), \(\psi_t=V\psi\) is \(U_t-V_x+[U,V]=0\) at each regular value of \(\lambda\). A spectral-parameter representation alone does not establish a Hamiltonian structure or completeness of inverse scattering.
fate: This is the established zero-curvature formulation; the relativistic elliptic models discussed next belong to the programme in \citet{cherednik1981quasiclassical}, submitted 8 August 1980 and published in 1981.

title: The third-stage unification slogan
notes: The Yang--Baxter equation is presented as the third stage, encompassing all or almost all integrable systems and connecting scattering with statistical mechanics.
statement: The diagram records a programme of constructions and limiting procedures between specified models. It is not a theorem that every system called integrable arises from a Yang--Baxter equation.
fate: \citet[Introduction]{belavin1980discrete} gives concrete scattering/discrete-symmetry constructions; it does not prove the unqualified universality slogan.

title: Elliptic linear systems for anisotropic vector equations
notes: The auxiliary vector \(E\) satisfies \(E_x=(J(\lambda-\alpha)V)\times E\), \(E_t=(J(\lambda)U)\times E\). The ensuing nonlinear system has \(U_x=(JV)\times U\) and a second line written with \(U_t\).
statement: An elliptic spectral parameter can enter an \(\mathfrak{so}_3\)-valued flat connection by identifying vectors with cross-product matrices. Compatibility requires the coefficient of each independent elliptic function in its curvature to vanish. The exact two-field system cannot be recovered from an unspecified elliptic matrix \(J(\lambda)\) and the repeated \(U\) in the second line alone.
reconstruction: The missing equality sign in the \(E_t\) line is syntactic; replacing the second \(U_t\) by \(V_t\) would be a mathematical conjecture about the intended system and is not silently adopted.
fate: The subject matches Cherednik’s relativistic quasiclassical models \citep[abstract and pp.~422--425]{cherednik1981quasiclassical}; this is a partial, not equation-by-equation, identification.
present_status: As of November 2026, the construction is identifiable at the level of elliptic zero-curvature models, but the exact notebook normalization is unresolved.

title: Landau–Lifshitz dynamics and scattering brackets
notes: The notes write \(U_t=U\times U_{xx}+(JU)\times U\) and say that Yang--Baxter theory supplies Hamiltonian and scattering brackets.
statement: For a smooth spin field of fixed length and a constant diagonal anisotropy matrix \(J\), this is an anisotropic Landau--Lifshitz equation, with sign determined by the spin Poisson bracket convention. A statement about brackets of scattering data additionally requires a chosen Lax representation and boundary conditions.
fate: Classical and quantum inverse-scattering constructions already precede this lecture; compare \citet{sklyaninfaddeev1978quantum}. The notebook does not specify the scattering-data bracket to be identified.

title: Unimodular torus charts and character--cocharacter duality
notes: The continuation writes \(x_i=\prod_j u_j^{a_{ij}}\), one-parameter groups \(x_i=t^{\lambda_i}\), and the value \(t^{\langle m,\lambda\rangle}\) of a monomial on such a group.
statement: For \(T=(\mathbb C^*)^n\), the character lattice \(M=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbb C^*)\) and cocharacter lattice \(N=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb C^*,T)\) are dual. In chosen bases, \(\chi^m(t^\lambda)=t^{\langle m,\lambda\rangle}\). The monomial change \(x_i=\prod_j u_j^{a_{ij}}\) is an isomorphism of tori precisely when \(A\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)\). An \(\mathbb A^n\) chart in a smooth toric compactification corresponds to a maximal cone generated by its cocharacter-basis columns.
reconstruction: Unimodularity distinguishes a chart isomorphism from a finite monomial covering. The statement concerns a chosen torus with its action, not arbitrary analytic compactifications.
fate: The exact pairing, monomial coordinate change, and associated cones are read in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}, published in 1977, and \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The fan compatibility condition
notes: Cones are generated by the columns of the chart matrix. Overlapping interiors force equality; a second statement applies the same requirement to faces.
statement: A finite collection of strongly convex rational cones defines a separated toric gluing when it is closed under faces and the intersection of every two cones is a face of each. Equivalently, relative interiors of all its cones are disjoint unless the cones coincide. Smoothness requires every cone to be generated by part of a lattice basis.
reconstruction: The second, facewise sentence is essential: disjoint interiors of maximal cones alone are insufficient. Including all faces makes the notebook's criterion the standard fan condition.
fate: This is the admissibility theorem in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; compare the systematic fan gluing in \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric}. It is established before the lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: The sigma-process example is one blow-up chart
notes: The substitution \(x_1=u_1u_2^{-1},\ x_2=u_2\), or \(u_1=x_1x_2,\ u_2=x_2\), is called a sigma-process.
statement: The map \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto(u_1,u_2)=(x_1x_2,x_2)\) is one affine chart of the blow-up of the origin in the \(u\)-plane; the other standard chart is needed for the complete blow-up. Torically, the modification subdivides the positive-quadrant cone by the ray \(e_1+e_2\). On the dense torus the displayed inverse is the stated unimodular monomial transformation.
reconstruction: The direction of the morphism and the need for the second chart are explicit; the inverse formula is not regular along \(u_2=0\) in the original plane.
fate: The standard toric modification construction is read in \citet[\S5 and the discussion of subdivisions]{danilov1978toric}; its unimodular chart interpretation is also in \citet[\S1]{khovanskii1977toroidal}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Completeness, the projective-plane fan, and toric classification
notes: The compactness criterion is that the cones cover the whole vector space. A three-ray drawing gives the projective plane, and the compactification is said to be determined up to an integral automorphism.
statement: The complex toric variety \(X_\Sigma\) is complete (equivalently compact analytically) exactly when \(|\Sigma|=N_\mathbb R\). The fan with rays \((1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1)\) and the three intervening two-dimensional cones gives \(\mathbb P^2\). Smooth complete toric varieties with their dense torus action are classified by smooth complete fans; allowing an automorphism of the torus identifies fans under \(\operatorname{GL}(N)\). Completeness alone does not assert projectivity.
reconstruction: The classification is equivariant and concerns valid fans. The projective-plane ray generators are reconstructed from the standard three-chart model shown schematically.
fate: The completeness equivalence is read in \citet[\S1, compactness theorem]{khovanskii1977toroidal}; \citet[\S5]{danilov1978toric} supplies the fan classification. Both precede 1981.
present_status: As of November 2026, the statement with the displayed hypotheses is established; the notebook occurrence is expository.

title: Exponential sums and complex Newton polytopes
notes: The proposed extension replaces Laurent polynomials by finite sums \(f(z)=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}c_\lambda e^{\langle z,\lambda\rangle}\), with \(\Lambda\subset\mathbb C^n\), and calls \(\operatorname{conv}(\Lambda)\) the Newton polyhedron.
statement: For a finite spectrum \(\Lambda\subset(\mathbb C^n)^*\), with nonzero coefficients on its support, the expression defines an entire exponential sum. Its complex Newton polytope is the real convex hull \(\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{2n}\) of that spectrum. The pairing in the exponential is complex bilinear; the associated real support function is \(h_\Gamma(z)=\max_{\lambda\in\Gamma}\operatorname{Re}\langle z,\lambda\rangle\). Integer real spectra recover Laurent polynomials after \(x_j=e^{z_j}\).
reconstruction: The real convex hull and the complex-bilinear pairing are distinguished. The logarithmic substitution is a covering map, so it changes finite torus counts into densities of infinitely many lifted roots.
fate: The definition is read at the opening of \citet[p.347]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}. The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the complex-spectrum formulation is established; it is the precise setting of the announced extension.

title: Asymptotic zero count for regular exponential systems
notes: For \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\), the notebook states \(N_F(R)=cV(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)R^n+O(R^{n-1})\), without recording the regularity condition or exact constant.
statement: Put \(\Gamma=\sum_i\Gamma_i\). For each face \(\Delta\) of \(\Gamma\), write \(\Delta=\sum_i\Delta_i\) and form the face sums \(f_i^\Delta\). Assume there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every face whose complex affine span has dimension less than \(n\), and every \(z\in\mathbb C^n\), \[\sum_i\frac{|f_i^\Delta(z)|}{\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda_i\cap\Delta_i}|e^{\langle z,\lambda\rangle}|}\geq\varepsilon.\] This is Kazarnovskii's regularity condition. Counting isolated common roots with multiplicity in the radius-\(R\) Euclidean ball, \[N_F(R)=\frac{\kappa_n n!}{(2\pi)^n}P_n(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)R^n+O(R^{n-1}),\] where \(\kappa_n\) is the volume of the real unit \(n\)-ball and \(P_n\) agrees with ordinary mixed volume for bodies in \(\mathbb R^n\).
reconstruction: The condition and normalization are imported from the publication. A system with common positive-dimensional zero components cannot be counted by the literal bare formula. For \(e^z-1\), \(P_1([0,1])=1\) gives \(N(R)=R/\pi+O(1)\), checking the constant. The actual notebook scan clearly has uppercase \(O\); the retrieved 1981 OCR renders that glyph ambiguously.
fate: This matches \citet[Definition 3 and Theorem 1, pp.348--349]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}, specialized to \(r=n\). The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the stated regular-system asymptotic is established. No claim is made for an arbitrary fixed system with the same spectra.

title: The face formula for pseudovolume
notes: The diagonal functional is a sum over real \(n\)-faces of volume times external angle times the area distortion of \(E^\perp\to iE\).
statement: For a convex polytope \(\Gamma\subset\mathbb C^n\), \[P_n(\Gamma)=\sum_{\dim_{\mathbb R} F=n}\operatorname{Vol}_n(F)\,\Omega(F)\,g(E_F),\qquad g(E)=\left|\det\bigl(\operatorname{pr}_{iE}|_{E^\perp}\bigr)\right|.\] Here \(E_F\) is the direction space of the face, and \(\Omega(F)\) is the solid angle of its exterior normal cone, normalized as a fraction of the unit ball in \(E_F^\perp\). In particular \(g(\mathbb R^n)=1\), while \(g(E)=0\) when \(E\) contains a complex line. The formula is unitarily invariant; for \(n>1\) it is not generally monotone under inclusion.
reconstruction: All face dimensions are real; the determinant is an absolute Euclidean Jacobian between equal-dimensional real spaces. For a lower-dimensional body its whole body can be a face and its normal cone can be a full orthogonal space.
fate: The exact face construction, complex-angle factor, and nonmonotonicity warning are read in \citet[\S1, Definition 1]{kazarnovskii1981zeros}. The notebook's projection is the transpose version of the same equal-dimensional projection determinant. The paper appeared in 1981 and records receipt on 6 November 1980; receipt is not treated as evidence of public circulation. The seminar report on 23 February 1981 is the verified oral occurrence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the face formula and its Hermitian dependence are established; ordinary real volume is only a special case.

title: Polarization and the real-spectrum specialization
notes: The multilinear \(V(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)\) is described through the single-polytope functional; it is ordinary mixed volume when all spectra are real. In one variable a perimeter appears.
statement: There is a symmetric Minkowski-multilinear polarization \(P_n(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_n)\) whose diagonal is the preceding face functional. For bodies in the same real form \(\mathbb R^n\subset\mathbb C^n\), it is ordinary mixed volume in the normalization \(V(K,\ldots,K)=\operatorname{Vol}_n(K)\). For \(n=1\), \(P_1\) is half the planar perimeter, with a line segment assigned perimeter twice its length. Thus the one-variable leading zero count is \(\operatorname{Perimeter}(\Gamma)R/(2\pi)\).
reconstruction: The polarization and semiperimeter normalization explain the unspecified constant in the notes. The statement is not ordinary \(2n\)-dimensional mixed volume of complex polytopes.

title: Smooth-boundary and Levi-form descriptions of pseudovolume

title: Support functions and the growth-indicatrix question of 2 March

title: The remark excluding coprime differential orders

title: Kodaira dimension and irregularity
notes: Viehweg defines \(\kappa\) using the graded algebra \(\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^0(X,\Omega_X^{n\otimes m})\) and \(q=\dim H^0(X,\Omega_X^1)\).
statement: For a smooth connected projective complex \(n\)-fold, let \(R(X,K_X)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}H^0(X,K_X^{\otimes m})\). If every positive-degree piece vanishes, \(\kappa(X)=-\infty\); otherwise \(\kappa(X)=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb C}R(X,K_X)-1\). Irregularity is \(q(X)=h^0(X,\Omega_X^1)=h^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\).
reconstruction: Smoothness, projectivity, the zero-ring exception, and transcendence degree rather than an unspecified degree are supplied.
fate: These conventions are given at the start of \citet[pp.~111--112]{esnault1981classification}, Bourbaki exposé 568, February 1981, explicitly named by the lecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Maximal irregularity at Kodaira dimension zero
notes: The table relates \(\kappa=0\), \(q=n\), and being birationally equivalent to an abelian variety; the direction of an arrow is unclear.
statement: If \(X\) is smooth projective over \(\mathbb C\), \(\kappa(X)=0\), and \(q(X)=\dim X\), then its Albanese map is birational onto an abelian variety. Conversely a variety birational to an abelian variety has these invariants.
reconstruction: The complete equivalence is the modern reconstruction; the manuscript arrow itself remains a palaeographic ambiguity.
fate: \citet[Thm.~1 and the adjacent table]{esnault1981classification} reports the Kawamata result before the seminar date. This is an exact subject match, although the notebook arrow is not silently read as an equivalence.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Irregular threefolds of Kodaira dimension zero
notes: For \(n=3\), \(\kappa=0\), and \(q=2\) or \(1\), the notes say there is an étale fibration and the fibre has \(\kappa=0\).
statement: For the smooth projective complex threefolds in the cited classification, the Albanese description becomes a product after a suitable finite étale base change, up to the birational modifications allowed in the theorem. The general fibre has dimension \(3-q\) and Kodaira dimension zero. Calling the map itself étale is impossible when its fibres have positive dimension.
reconstruction: Étale refers to the base change and local trivialization, not to a positive-dimensional-fibre morphism.
fate: \citet[Thm.~2 and table, pp.~112--114]{esnault1981classification} is the explicitly identified source. The note compresses birational and finite-cover qualifications into the phrase about étaleness.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Waldhausen’s K-theory programme for diffeomorphism spaces
notes: Kassel relates the homotopy type of a diffeomorphism group to the algebraic K-theory of a loop-space ring, invoking Waldhausen and homotopy rings.
statement: For a connected pointed CW space \(X\), algebraic K-theory of spaces, \(A(X)\), is a homotopy-theoretic construction involving retractive spaces over \(X\), or equivalently appropriate modules over the suspension ring spectrum of \(\Omega X\). Its relation to stable pseudoisotopy and stable smooth h-cobordisms is not an identity between an arbitrary diffeomorphism group and the ordinary K-theory of \(\mathbb Z[\pi_1X]\).
reconstruction: The distinction between A-theory and ordinary group-ring K-theory is explicit; no unstated stable-range theorem is supplied.
fate: \citet[pp.~35--60]{waldhausen1978topological} appeared in the proceedings of the 1976 Stanford symposium, published 1978. \citet[Introduction and §1]{kassel1983stabilisation} develops the homotopy-ring and stabilization context, received after this lecture and published in 1983. No exact diffeomorphism-space equivalence is stated in this notebook.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Quillen’s plus construction and homotopy rings
notes: The notes compare Quillen’s plus construction for rings with a homotopy-ring construction and mention maps between the corresponding classifying spaces.
statement: For a unital discrete ring \(R\), the positive K-groups are \(K_i(R)=\pi_i(BGL(R)^+)\), \(i\ge1\), with the plus construction killing the stable elementary subgroup. Passing to a ring structure defined only up to homotopy requires coherent multiplication and a compatible homotopical K-theory construction; a bare nonassociative operation up to an unspecified homotopy does not suffice.
fate: The ordinary construction is Quillen’s earlier theory; \citet[§1]{kassel1983stabilisation} provides the relevant homotopy-theoretic refinement. Its 1983 publication is a partial identification of the discussion, not a proof that every diagram in the shorthand is the same theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Soulé’s zeta-value bounds for the orders of K-groups
notes: Under a separate Soulé heading, for even \(i\ge2\) the notes bound \(|K_{2i-2}(\mathbb Z)|\) and \(|K_{2i-1}(\mathbb Z)|\) below by the numerator and denominator of \(\zeta(1-i)\). They cite Inventiones, February 1980, and a method involving topoi.
statement: Write \(|\zeta(1-i)|=a_i/b_i\) in lowest terms, \(a_i,b_i>0\), with even \(i\ge2\). The modern finite-order formulas imply \(|K_{2i-2}(\mathbb Z)|\ge a_i\) and \(|K_{2i-1}(\mathbb Z)|\ge b_i\). Absolute numerator is necessary when the zeta value is negative. Étale Chern classes and arithmetic cohomology are part of the source context; the cryptic date does not identify an exact theorem by itself.
reconstruction: The sign convention for numerator and the separation between present validity and historical attribution are supplied.
fate: Soulé’s arithmetic paper was published in October 1979, not February 1980 \citep{soule1979k}. His 1978 thesis gives related lower bounds with prime restrictions \citep[Introduction]{soule1978thesis}. Complete formulas, including the factors at 2, are recorded in \citet[Cor.~95 and Table~5.1]{weibel2005rings}. The cited later formulas verify the inequalities but do not establish that their full strength was proved in the unidentified February reference.
present_status: As of November 2026, these numerical lower bounds follow from established arithmetic K-theory formulas. Exact attribution of the full displayed bounds to the manuscript’s February 1980 reference remains unresolved.

title: Incompressible Euler flow as geodesic motion
notes: The quadratic form \(\frac12\int|v|^2\) on divergence-free vector fields is extended by left translations to volume-preserving diffeomorphisms; its geodesics are ideal-fluid flows.
statement: For a compact oriented Riemannian manifold without boundary, or with the usual impermeable boundary condition, equip volume-preserving diffeomorphisms with the right-invariant weak \(L^2\) metric in the usual material-to-spatial convention. Its smooth geodesics have Eulerian velocity satisfying \(u_t+\nabla_u u=-\nabla p\), \(\operatorname{div}u=0\). An inverse-map convention interchanges left and right.
reconstruction: The manifold, boundary condition, smooth lifespan, and right-translation convention are supplied.

title: Hamiltonian reduction and coadjoint-orbit symplectic forms
notes: The invariant kinetic energy on \(T^*G\) projects to \(\mathfrak g^*\), whose coadjoint orbits carry the Kirillov form.
statement: For a finite-dimensional Lie group, an invariant Hamiltonian on its cotangent bundle reduces under the lifted translation action to a Lie--Poisson Hamiltonian on \(\mathfrak g^*\). Its symplectic leaves are coadjoint orbits with the Kirillov--Kostant--Souriau form. Infinite-dimensional fluid versions require a chosen regular dual, functional setting, and smoothness domain.
reconstruction: The note’s phrase that the Kirillov form descends is interpreted through reduction; it is not a globally nondegenerate form on all of the dual.
fate: The Euler-group reduction is part of \citet{arnold1966geometrie}. The Vlasov application is developed by \citet{marsdenweinstein1982hamiltonian}, received August 1981 and published March 1982.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: The Vlasov Lie–Poisson bracket
notes: The group of canonical transformations is said to produce the Vlasov equation, with the parenthetical phrase cold plasma.
statement: On canonical phase space \(T^*\mathbb R^d\), identified with \((x,v)\) in unit-mass coordinates, the Lie--Poisson bracket is \(\{F,G\}(f)=\int f\{\delta F/\delta f,\delta G/\delta f\}_{x,v}\,dx\,dv\), with a consistent overall sign convention. A rigorous algebraic core consists of smooth compactly supported densities and cylindrical polynomial functionals built from pairings with compactly supported smooth test functions. For more general functionals, smooth variational derivatives and decay sufficient for all integrals and integrations by parts are assumed. The kinetic-plus-self-field Hamiltonian formally yields Vlasov evolution within its smooth domain; this construction alone is not an analytic existence theorem and does not require a monokinetic ansatz.
fate: The pure Vlasov functional bracket is already explicit in \citet[p.~385, Eq.~(12)]{morrison1980maxwell}, received August and published December 1980, before this lecture. In canonical momentum variables or unit-mass normalization it is the displayed formula. \citet[pp.~235--236]{weinsteinmorrison1981comments} corrects the mass factors and the separate magnetic coupling, whose original form failed Jacobi. \citet{marsdenweinstein1982hamiltonian} subsequently gives the geometric coadjoint/gauge construction; that later implementation is not the first occurrence of the pure bracket.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

notes: Adding local degrees of freedom and a gauge group is said to lead to further equations, including Yang--Mills.
statement: The identifiable extension couples a distribution on particle phase space with internal gauge charge to a gauge field, using a reduced Hamiltonian bracket and constraints. The note does not specify a gauge group, charge orbit, field variables, or an exact Yang--Mills--Vlasov bracket.
fate: \citet[abstract]{marsdenweinstein1982hamiltonian} explicitly states applicability to the Yang--Mills--Vlasov system. This verifies the direction of development, not a formula absent from the manuscript.

title: Density and the incomplete compressible-fluid Hamiltonian claim
notes: The note says vorticity must be specified before a Hamiltonian formalism exists, then refers to bundles over the group carrying density.
statement: Compressible-fluid Hamiltonian descriptions require the advected mass density in addition to momentum; a semidirect-product or equivalent cotangent construction provides this. Fixing vorticity is not a general prerequisite for a Hamiltonian formulation. No particular bracket or bundle is specified here.
fate: The contextual fluid geometry is \citet{arnold1966geometrie}; the nearby compressibility work is discussed more explicitly in record 527. The incomplete vorticity phrase is not identified with a published theorem.

title: Elastic collisions and the homogeneous Boltzmann equation
notes: The collision integral is quadratic in \(f\), with \(v^{\prime},w^{\prime}=(v+w\pm|v-w|n)/2\), \(|n|=1\), and kernel \(g=|v-w|\,d\sigma/d\Omega\).
statement: For equal-mass elastic collisions in three dimensions, the displayed postcollision velocities preserve total momentum and kinetic energy. The spatially homogeneous Boltzmann equation is \(\partial_tf=Q(f,f)\), where the angular and relative-speed kernel is nonnegative and the integral is interpreted under the integrability or cancellation hypotheses appropriate to it. Molecular chaos is the modelling assumption behind the product of one-particle densities.
fate: \citet[§1]{bobylev1984exact} gives the collision equation and conventions. This is standard background, not a theorem identifying a deterministic hard-sphere limit for arbitrary times.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Inverse-power potentials and Maxwell molecules
notes: For \(V(r)=\alpha r^{-s}\), the collision kernel is \(\widetilde g(\mu)|v-w|^{1-4/s}\). The case \(s=4\) depends only on the angle.
statement: For repulsive inverse-power pair potentials, homogeneity yields the displayed relative-speed exponent in the usual classical scattering convention in three dimensions. The inverse-fourth-power potential is the Maxwell-molecule case. This speed independence does not imply that the angular kernel is integrable; an angular cutoff is a separate assumption.
fate: \citet[§1]{bobylev1984exact} distinguishes true Maxwell molecules from their cutoff or pseudo-Maxwell models. The distinction matters to the later compactness and normalization statements.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: The Bobylev Fourier identity
notes: When the kernel depends only on angle, Fourier transformation greatly simplifies the equation and gives exact solutions.
statement: For a homogeneous Maxwell model with integrable angular kernel \(b\), let \(\phi(k)=\int e^{-ik\cdot v}f(v)\,dv\). Then \(\partial_t\phi(k)=\int_{S^2}b(\widehat k\cdot\sigma)[\phi(k^+)\phi(k^-)-\phi(k)\phi(0)]\,d\sigma\), where \(k^\pm=(k\pm|k|\sigma)/2\). Noncutoff versions require the corresponding cancellation interpretation.
reconstruction: The Fourier variables and angular-cutoff hypothesis make the shorthand precise.
fate: Bobylev’s Fourier method and exact-solution papers appeared in 1975, before this seminar. \citet[§1 and references~4--8]{bobylev1984exact} reproduces the identity and its chronology.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Gaussian convolution symmetry
notes: Convolving with a Gaussian density does not change the equation.
statement: If \(f(t)\) solves the homogeneous Maxwell-molecule equation and \(G_a\) is a fixed centred normalized isotropic Gaussian, then \(G_a*f(t)\) solves the same equation, whenever both are in the relevant solution class. In Fourier variables this follows from \(|k^+|^2+|k^-|^2=|k|^2\). The variance is constant in time.
fate: This symmetry belongs to Bobylev’s Maxwell Fourier method \citep[§1]{bobylev1984exact}. The statement is not a symmetry of an arbitrary velocity-dependent collision kernel or of an arbitrary time-dependent convolution.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Maxwellians and linearization
notes: The stationary family is \(f_M=Ae^{-\alpha|v-v_0|^2}\), called three-parameter for the blocks \(A,\alpha,v_0\). Substitution \(f=f_M(1+F)\) gives the displayed linear collision operator.
statement: For \(A,\alpha>0\) and \(v_0\in\mathbb R^3\), these equilibria have five scalar parameters. Linearizing gives \(\mathcal LF=f_M^{-1}[Q(f_MF,f_M)+Q(f_M,f_MF)]\). With detailed balance and the appropriate domain, \(\mathcal L\) is nonpositive and self-adjoint in \(L^2(f_M\,dv)\); its nullspace is spanned by \(1,v_1,v_2,v_3,|v|^2\) for a nondegenerate collision kernel.
reconstruction: The three named blocks contain five real scalar parameters; this repairs a counting ambiguity rather than introducing a new equilibrium family.
fate: \citet[§§1,3]{bobylev1984exact} treats the Maxwellian and its spectral linearization. The notebook’s integral has specialized the equilibrium scale, mean, and normalization.

title: Triangular linearization of the isotropic Maxwell hierarchy
notes: For isotropic \(f(|v|^2)\) and \(s=4\), an infinite system of ordinary differential equations can be transformed into a linear system. The surrounding text mentions general solutions among rapidly decaying functions and says other cases are unknown.
statement: In the normalized isotropic cutoff Maxwell model, the Fourier or moment coefficients satisfy a triangular nonlinear hierarchy. On Bobylev’s specified analytic coefficient class, a triangular polynomial change of coefficients conjugates it to \(\dot y_n=-\lambda_n y_n\), \(n\ge2\), with \(\lambda_n=\int_0^1p(s)[1-s^n-(1-s)^n]\,ds\) and nonnegative integrable angular weight \(p\). The analytic class and invertibility estimates are essential; the result is not a blanket linearization for every Schwartz density or every anisotropic model.
reconstruction: The result is stated for the analytic class used by the primary proof; a larger unrestricted rapidly decaying class is not asserted.
fate: \citet{bobylev1981poincare} was received 4 August 1980 and appeared in 1981. A full explicit proof is in \citet[§4, theorem and Eqs.~(4.8)--(4.14)]{bobylev1984exact}, received May 1984. Its nonresonance and function-space restrictions qualify the notebook’s broad wording.
present_status: As of November 2026, this specified isotropic linearization is established. The manuscript’s phrase unknown in other cases is historical and too unspecific to define an additional open problem.

title: Countably many nonlinear invariants of relaxation
notes: The notes claim infinitely many conservation laws and exact solutions.
statement: For non-equilibrium solutions in the preceding normal-coordinate class, fix an index \(m\) with \(y_m\ne0\). Quantities \(|y_n|^{1/\lambda_n}/|y_m|^{1/\lambda_m}\) are constant wherever defined. Finite sets of nonzero normal coordinates also generate explicit special-solution families. These nonlinear functionals differ from the five linear collision invariants expressing mass, momentum, and energy.
fate: \citet[§4, Corollaries~1--2, Eqs.~(4.15)--(4.21)]{bobylev1984exact} gives these consequences of the hierarchy already announced in \citet{bobylev1981poincare}.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: The spatially inhomogeneous and hydrodynamic-limit programme
notes: The spatially inhomogeneous equation is important, and a limiting mean-free-path regime gives Navier--Stokes.
statement: The schematic kinetic-to-fluid statement requires a specified Knudsen scaling, collision model, boundary conditions, preparation of initial data, and solution class. Depending on the scaling, limiting equations can instead be compressible or incompressible Euler, acoustic, or diffusive systems. The notebook gives none of these choices.
fate: \citet[§5]{bobylev1984exact} discusses the limitations of formal hydrodynamic expansions. It does not identify a single rigorous limit theorem with the brief seminar sentence.

title: The Hermitian sum spectral problem
notes: Three decreasing lists \(x,y,z\) satisfy \(\sum_i(x_i+y_i-z_i)=0\). The problem is to characterize when they are spectra of Hermitian \(X,Y,Z\) with \(X+Y=Z\).
statement: For real weakly decreasing \(n\)-tuples \(x,y,z\), characterize the existence of complex Hermitian \(n\times n\) matrices \(X,Y\) whose eigenvalue lists are \(x,y\) and whose sum has eigenvalue list \(z\). Trace equality is necessary and is retained in the final characterization.
fate: Lidskii announced the recursive answer in \citet{lidskii1982spectral}, received October 1981 and published April 1982. A complete resolution follows from the work connected by \citet[§1]{knutsontao1999honeycomb}, first circulated July 1998 and published in 1999.
present_status: As of November 2026, the Horn problem is solved by the recursive inequalities, equivalently by the honeycomb and representation-theoretic criteria.

title: The recursive Horn inequalities
notes: Triples of increasing index lists are declared consistent by a trace-of-indices equality and inequalities for smaller consistent triples; the final answer is \(\sum z_{c_j}\le\sum x_{a_j}+\sum y_{b_j}\).
statement: For \(1\le r\le n\), let \(U_r^n\) consist of triples \(I,J,K\) of \(r\)-subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(\sum I+\sum J-\sum K=r(r+1)/2\). Set \(T_1^n=U_1^n\); for \(r>1\), retain \((I,J,K)\in U_r^n\) exactly when every \(p<r\) and \((F,G,H)\in T_p^r\) satisfy \(\sum_{f\in F}i_f+\sum_{g\in G}j_g\le\sum_{h\in H}k_h+p(p+1)/2\). Hermitian realizability is equivalent to trace equality and \(\sum_{k\in K}z_k\le\sum_{i\in I}x_i+\sum_{j\in J}y_j\) for all \(r<n\) and \((I,J,K)\in T_r^n\).
reconstruction: The recursion requires \(p<r\) (the notebook writes only \(\ell<n\)), and the final answer also requires the trace equality already stated on the preceding page.
fate: \citet{lidskii1982spectral} is the exact short announcement. \citet{dayso1998spectrum} documents the absence of a published supporting proof at that stage; \citet[§1 and the saturation theorem]{knutsontao1999honeycomb} gives the later route completing Horn’s conjecture.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Convolution of orbital measures
notes: The notes add that probability can also be written as a convolution.
statement: For fixed spectra \(x,y\), take independent Haar-distributed unitary conjugates of their diagonal matrices. The law of the matrix sum is the convolution of the corresponding orbital probability measures on Hermitian matrices; its spectral pushforward is supported on the Horn polytope. The source gives no density or probability formula beyond this construction.
fate: The spectral-sum context is \citet{dayso1998spectrum}; identifying a convolution is elementary once the orbital measures are defined. No explicit multiplicity or density algorithm is attributed to the one-line remark.

title: Barotropic compressible Euler equations
notes: The notes give \(u_t+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla p\), \(\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0\), \(p=p(\rho)\), exemplified by \(p=A\rho^\gamma\), and separately say \(T\) is constant.
statement: For smooth positive density and a smooth barotropic pressure law, these are the compressible inviscid mass and momentum equations. Strict hyperbolicity of the acoustic part requires \(p^{\prime}(\rho)>0\). Barotropy does not require constant temperature: the polytropic ideal-gas law generally models an isentropic, nonisothermal regime, while the isothermal ideal-gas case has \(\gamma=1\).
reconstruction: Positivity, smoothness, hyperbolicity, and the separation of barotropy from isothermality are supplied.
fate: This is the continuum model underlying \citet{ebin1977slightly}. Gelfand’s heating objection identifies a limitation of the simplified thermodynamic model, not a mathematical contradiction in barotropic Euler theory.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Characteristics and the onset of a scalar shock
notes: For \(u_t+cu_x=0\), \(u=f(x-ct)\); for \(u_t+uu_x=0\), \(u=f(x-ut)\). The drawing shows a falling flank overturning, and says shocks necessarily occur.
statement: For scalar Burgers data \(u(0,x)=f(x)\in C^1\) with bounded derivative, the classical solution is parametrized by \(x=\xi+tf(\xi)\), \(u=f(\xi)\), while \(1+tf^{\prime}(\xi)>0\). If \(\inf f^{\prime}<0\), its first gradient catastrophe is at \(-1/\inf f^{\prime}\); nondecreasing data do not form this forward-time compression shock. Constant data also remain smooth.
fate: The characteristic calculation is classical background to the entropy theory of \citet{kruzhkov1970first}, received April 1969 and published 1970. The unconditional assertion that nonlinear hyperbolic equations always require shocks is false.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Conservation form and entropy selection
notes: After characteristic crossing one should write \(u_t+\frac12(u^2)_x=0\) and define discontinuous solutions.
statement: Bounded weak solutions satisfy the distributional conservation law, but that condition alone does not select a unique evolution. The scalar entropy solution obeys the Kruzhkov inequalities; a shock between constant states has Rankine--Hugoniot speed \((u_-+u_+)/2\), and for convex Burgers flux a decreasing jump is admissible.
fate: \citet{kruzhkov1970first} proves existence, uniqueness, and stability in the bounded entropy class. The source’s request to understand discontinuities is thus an exposition of an established theory, not an unresolved uniqueness question.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Zakharov’s matrix Hopf equation
notes: Zakharov says \(U_t+UU_x=0\), with matrix \(U\), can also be integrated completely.
statement: For matrix-valued \(U\), multiplication order matters: \(UU_x\) is generally not \(\frac12(U^2)_x\). The source provides no spectral assumptions, initial-data class, solution formula, or definition of complete integration. Diagonal or mutually commuting reductions reduce to scalar characteristic equations, but that is only a restricted case.
fate: The nearby scalar theory does not certify the unqualified matrix claim. Searches for matrix Hopf and Zakharov noncommutative hydrodynamic systems did not identify a primary theorem with exactly these unspecified hypotheses. No general integrability theorem is inferred.
present_status: As of November 2026, the exact general matrix-integration assertion in this note remains unidentified; scalar commuting reductions are elementary and do not settle it.
speaker: V. E. Zakharov

title: Expansion of gas into vacuum
notes: For a vessel initially divided into gas and vacuum, removing the partition is said to produce a system of shocks moving back and forth.
statement: The initial expansion of a positive-pressure gas into vacuum in the standard one-dimensional isentropic Riemann problem is described by a rarefaction toward vacuum. Later wall reflections depend on the equation of state, boundary conditions, and geometry. The diagram alone does not determine a universal shock-train evolution or equilibration theorem.
fate: The displayed compressible equations permit both compression and expansion waves; the scalar entropy context is \citet{kruzhkov1970first}. No exact vessel problem or solution theorem was found that warrants the notebook’s unqualified description.

title: The hyperbolic-plane nonimmersion analogy
notes: The notes connect the preceding shock discussion to the assertion that the Lobachevsky plane does not embed in \(\mathbb R^3\).
statement: The classical geometric obstruction is that the complete constant-negative-curvature hyperbolic plane has no smooth isometric immersion into Euclidean three-space. Topological or smooth embeddings without preservation of the metric exist. The notebook supplies no argument connecting this theorem to the gas example.
fate: The intended geometric result is \citet{hilbert1901flachen}; the primary AMS access attempt was blocked, so the bibliography records that limitation. The isometric and completeness qualifications are indispensable and the asserted causal link to shocks is not established.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified Hilbert nonimmersion theorem is classical; the unqualified embedding sentence and the suggested gas analogy are not valid as a proof.

title: The slightly compressible to incompressible limit
notes: Krein says that with density close to one, a parameter limit gives incompressible-fluid solutions.
statement: For the smooth slightly compressible models and compatible, suitably prepared initial data of Ebin’s theorem, solutions approach the incompressible motion on a common time interval where the latter remains smooth. A small Mach parameter, appropriate control of acoustic oscillations, and boundary compatibility are essential; arbitrary data and passage through shock formation are not covered.
reconstruction: This is a calibrated description of the source theorem, not a new quantified convergence statement without its original hypotheses.
fate: The identifiable result is \citet{ebin1977slightly}, published in January 1977, before this lecture. The opened Annals record verifies the source and its strong-constraint interpretation; the notebook does not state the exact function spaces or convergence norm.

title: Internal energy in material coordinates
notes: For the Jacobian \(g(x)\) of the flow map, the potential energy is \[\int_\Omega\int_1^{g^{-1}(x)}p(\rho)\rho^{-2}\,d\rho\,dx.\]
statement: With unit reference mass density, write the material flow as \(\eta(X)\), its positive Jacobian as \(J(X)\), and \(\rho(\eta(X))=J(X)^{-1}\). If specific internal energy obeys \(e^{\prime}(\rho)=p(\rho)/\rho^2\), then \(\int e(J^{-1})\,dX\) is the potential energy up to an additive constant. In Eulerian coordinates the same energy is \(\int \rho e(\rho)\,dx\).
reconstruction: The reference measure and distinction between specific energy and energy density are supplied explicitly.
fate: This is the mechanical energy interpretation used in the strongly constrained flow setting of \citet{ebin1977slightly}. The formula is consistent once the integral is read in material coordinates.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: The unspecific viscous-fluid extension
notes: The notes say the same exists for a viscous fluid, following Arnold.
statement: Viscosity adds a dissipative stress and destroys conservation of the inviscid Hamiltonian in general. A geometric formulation can still be given, but the sentence does not specify whether it refers to a manifold description, a limit theorem, or a Hamiltonian structure with extra variables.
fate: \citet{arnold1966geometrie} supplies the ideal-fluid geometric context; it does not make a viscous equation an energy-conserving geodesic flow by this sentence alone.
present_status: As of November 2026, the intended viscous analogue remains unspecified in this record.

title: A descending step for a polynomially regularized Burgers equation
notes: Gelfand asks what happens to a descending step profile for \(u_t+uu_x+p(\partial_x)u=0\), with \(p\) a polynomial. The final sentence says KdV continually sheds solitons.
statement: Long-time behaviour depends on the polynomial and on the solution concept: \(p=0\) gives entropy shocks, \(p(D)=-\nu D^2\), \(\nu>0\), gives viscous smoothing and travelling shocks, and a real cubic dispersive term gives the KdV dispersive-shock problem. Some polynomial symbols cause linear ill-posedness. The notes prescribe neither coefficients nor admissible class, so there is no single well-posed universal evolution question.
fate: For the KdV subcase, \citet{gurevichpitaevskii1974shock}, submitted April 1973, Russian publication 1973 and English 1974, describes the expanding modulated oscillatory zone with a soliton edge. This is a concrete prior result, not an answer for every polynomial.
present_status: As of November 2026, several specified subcases are established; the unrestricted polynomial question remains an underspecified programme, not a newly indexed open conjecture.

title: The semigroup of indefinite contractions
notes: For \(J=\operatorname{diag}(-I_p,I_q)\), a matrix \(A\) is a J-contraction when \(\langle Ax,Ax\rangle_J\le\langle x,x\rangle_J\). Such matrices form a semigroup.
statement: The inequality is \(A^*JA\le J\). If both \(A,B\) satisfy it, then \((AB)^*J(AB)=B^*A^*JAB\le B^*JB\le J\). The full matrix semigroup can include singular matrices; its invertible part is the part naturally compared with semigroups inside a complex Lie group.
fate: This is an elementary model for the constructions in \citet[§§3,6]{olshanskii1981cones}, received December 1980 and published in 1981. The singular boundary must not be conflated with the group-contained semigroup \(G\exp(iC)\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Compression semigroups of domains
notes: Examples are hyperbolic motions taking a half-plane into itself, and transformations of the compact dual of a bounded symmetric domain \(D\) taking \(D\) into itself. The matrix ball gives J-contractions.
statement: For a fixed domain \(D\) in a homogeneous space and an ambient transformation group, the set \(\{g:gD\subseteq D\}\) is a semigroup. For a Hermitian symmetric domain embedded in its compact dual, the connected complex group supplies the compression semigroup identified with the maximal-cone Olshanskii semigroup in the cited theorem. Matrix-ball realizations connect this geometry with appropriately normalized indefinite contractions.
reconstruction: The ambient group, connected component, and distinction from all holomorphic self-maps are made explicit.
fate: \citet[§6, Thm.~6.2]{olshanskii1981cones} proves the symmetric-domain identification. The elementary closure property applies also to the real half-plane example, but does not classify arbitrary domain-preserving maps.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Contractive involutive-semigroup representations
notes: The notes require \(T(ab)=T(a)T(b)\), \(T(a^\#)=T(a)^*\), and \(\|T(a)\|\le1\), where \((ab)^\#=b^\#a^\#\).
statement: A representation in the category used here is a continuous nondegenerate homomorphism of a topological involutive semigroup into bounded Hilbert-space contractions, respecting the involution. For a unital semigroup one takes \(T(1)=I\); weak operator continuity is sufficient in the primary definition and yields strong continuity in the setting considered.
fate: The exact definition appears in \citet[§4.2]{olshanskii1981cones}. Continuity and nondegeneracy are necessary category qualifications absent from the abbreviated notebook list.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Tensor-power representations of ordinary contractions
notes: For contractions on \(V=\mathbb C^n\), tensor powers give analytic representations indexed by sequences; anti-analytic representations also occur.
statement: The tensor-power action \(A\mapsto A^{\otimes m}\) restricts to the Schur modules \(S_\lambda V\), indexed by partitions \(\lambda\vdash m\) with at most \(n\) rows, and remains contractive. Conjugating gives antiholomorphic examples. These are polynomial holomorphic representations; the notebook does not justify classifying every continuous involutive-semigroup representation by these partitions alone.
reconstruction: The sequences are interpreted as partitions for polynomial representations, without extending the claim to an unrestricted continuous category.
fate: The examples motivate the analytic category in \citet[Introduction and §4]{olshanskii1981cones}. Ordinary matrix-contraction representations and the later \(\Gamma(C_{\min})\) theorem must be kept distinct.

title: The Hermitian criterion for invariant proper cones
notes: A convex adjoint-invariant cone with nonempty interior exists in a simple real Lie algebra exactly when it is of Hermitian type.
statement: For a noncompact simple real Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\), the existence of a nonzero closed convex pointed generating adjoint-invariant cone is equivalent to \(\mathfrak g\) being of Hermitian type. Nonempty interior alone is insufficient: \(\mathfrak g\) itself is an invariant convex cone. For \(\mathfrak g=\mathfrak k\oplus\mathfrak p\), the Hermitian condition is \(\dim Z(\mathfrak k)=1\).
reconstruction: Closedness, pointedness, generating property, and noncompactness are supplied.
fate: \citet[Thm.~1.2]{olshanskii1981cones} states the Vinberg--Kostant criterion and specifies the nondegenerate cone convention. This is explicitly attributed earlier work, even though its use in the speaker’s paper is new.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: The list of simple Hermitian real forms
notes: The list contains \(\mathfrak{su}(p,q)\), \(\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb R)\), \(\mathfrak{so}^*(2n)\), \(\mathfrak{so}(2,n)\), and two exceptional forms.
statement: The noncompact simple Hermitian families are \(\mathfrak{su}(p,q)\) for \(p,q\ge1\), \(\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb R)\) for \(n\ge1\), \(\mathfrak{so}^*(2n)\) for \(n\ge3\), and \(\mathfrak{so}(2,n)\) for \(n=1\) or \(n\ge3\), together with \(\mathfrak e_{6(-14)}\) and \(\mathfrak e_{7(-25)}\), with low-rank isomorphisms identified. In particular \(\mathfrak{so}(2,2)\) is semisimple rather than simple.
reconstruction: Exceptional signatures and the low-rank simplicity qualification are supplied.
fate: The criterion and root-theoretic conventions are in \citet[§1]{olshanskii1981cones}; the exceptional names expand the source’s shorthand.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Minimal and maximal cones after choosing an orientation
notes: There are unique \(C_{\min}\subset C_{\max}\), and a Cartan-subalgebra description, with attribution to Vinberg, Olshanskii, and Paneitz.
statement: After choosing a positive orientation in the one-dimensional centre of the maximal compact algebra, the positive invariant proper cones have a unique minimal and maximal member. Their negatives give the opposite orientation, so uniqueness without a sign choice is false. Intersection with a compact Cartan subspace identifies the intermediate cones with Weyl-invariant cones between the corresponding root-theoretic extrema.
reconstruction: A positive central direction, and hence an orientation of the cone, is fixed before stating uniqueness.
fate: \citet[Thms.~1.5,1.7,1.9 and Cor.~1.6]{olshanskii1981cones} gives the precise bounds and classification, distinguishing Vinberg’s earlier maximal cone from the new Cartan-cone description. The paper was received 4 December 1980.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Global semigroups from Hermitian invariant cones
notes: For every cone under discussion, \(\Gamma(C)=G\exp(iC)\) is a semigroup inside \(G_{\mathbb C}\).
statement: Let \(\mathfrak g\) be a noncompact simple Hermitian real Lie algebra, \(G_{\mathbb C}\) a connected complex Lie group with Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}\), and \(G\) its connected analytic subgroup with Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\). For a closed pointed generating adjoint-invariant cone \(C\subset\mathfrak g\), \(G\exp(iC)\) is a closed semigroup, and polar multiplication gives a homeomorphism \(G\times C\to\Gamma(C)\). Appropriate universal covers are used for representations that do not descend to this \(G\).
reconstruction: The Lie-group, cone, and covering hypotheses are stated explicitly.
fate: This is \citet[Thm.~3.5 and §4.1]{olshanskii1981cones}, after identifying the paper’s cone in \(i\mathfrak g\) with \(iC\). The theorem does not claim this global polar description for arbitrary Lie algebras or arbitrary convex cones.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Local semigroups for general invariant cones
notes: A weaker local version is said to hold for every Lie algebra.
statement: If \(M\) is a connected finite-dimensional Lie group and \(C\) a closed pointed generating invariant convex cone in its Lie algebra, the germ at the identity of \(\exp(C\cap U)\), with \(U\) shrinking to zero, is a local semigroup. This is a statement about products sufficiently near the identity, not automatic global closure of an exponential image.
fate: \citet[Thm.~3.3]{olshanskii1981cones} proves this assertion independently of the Hermitian global theorem.
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: The representation cone and highest-weight condition
notes: The note defines \(C(T)\) by a nonpositivity condition on infinitesimal generators and says it is nontrivial exactly for highest-weight representations.
statement: For a strongly continuous unitary representation \(\pi\), use the self-adjoint closures to define \(C_\pi=\{Y\in\mathfrak g:i\,d\pi(Y)\le0\}\). For a nontrivial irreducible unitary representation of the simply connected Hermitian group, a nonzero such cone, with its orientation fixed, characterizes a unitary highest-weight representation; the opposite orientation interchanges highest and lowest weight. The trivial representation has \(C_\pi=\mathfrak g\) and is a separate exception.
reconstruction: The infinitesimal generator, operator closure, irreducibility, exclusion of the trivial case, and orientation are supplied.
fate: \citet[Thms.~2.2,2.5]{olshanskii1981cones} gives the exact nontriviality, irreducibility, and sign qualifications. The paper works in \(i\mathfrak g\); the formula here pulls that convention back to \(\mathfrak g\).
present_status: As of November 2026, the qualified statement above is established; no new open problem is inferred from the omissions in the notebook.

title: Holomorphic extension and the contractive representation category
notes: A highest-weight representation extends holomorphically to \(\Gamma(C(T))\), called the exact extension domain, and there is a category equivalence.
statement: For a fixed positive invariant proper cone \(C\), unitary representations satisfying \(C\subset C_\pi\) extend uniquely to contractive involutive representations on the appropriate covering semigroup, holomorphic on its interior, with \(T(g\exp(iY))=\pi(g)\exp(i,d\pi(Y))\). Restriction is an equivalence of the corresponding categories. The cone \(C_\pi\) is maximal for contractive extension in this setting, not necessarily for all analytic continuations of every individual matrix coefficient.
reconstruction: The cone condition and the word contractive make precise both the category and the maximality assertion.
fate: \citet[Thms.~4.5--4.6 and Thm.~2.9]{olshanskii1981cones} provides the extension, uniqueness, and direct-integral/category formulation. The source’s phrase all highest-weight representations requires the compatibility condition with the chosen cone.

title: Holomorphic–antiholomorphic factorization for the minimal cone
notes: Irreducible representations are said to be tensor products of holomorphic and antiholomorphic irreducible representations.
statement: For the involutive semigroup associated with the minimal positive cone, in the continuous contractive category and on the cover specified by the theorem, every irreducible representation is the tensor product of a holomorphic highest-weight extension and the conjugate of another such extension. The theorem as checked does not assert the same unrestricted formulation for every intermediate cone.
reconstruction: The minimal-cone hypothesis is restored from the primary theorem.
fate: This is the exact scope of \citet[Cor.~5.8]{olshanskii1981cones}, whose notation explicitly has \(C_{\min}\). The notebook has dropped that qualifier.

title: Gelfand’s request to go beyond semisimple groups
notes: Gelfand objects to restricting the theory to simple or semisimple algebras, especially for infinite-dimensional representation theory.
statement: This is a programme to extend invariant-cone and semigroup methods beyond the finite-dimensional semisimple setting. No class of nonsemisimple or infinite-dimensional groups, topology, cone condition, or target theorem is specified.
fate: \citet[Introduction]{olshanskii1981cones} already discusses an oscillator example as motivation. That overlap is thematic and does not solve an unspecified universal extension problem.
